A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with matching core definitions, theoretical results and experiments. Their main texts, appendices, equations, tables and figures are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on aggregation, network stability and distribution shifts using ModelNet40, Polarity and Amazon reviews, including appendix results.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and adds attention-network experiments and predictive performance comparisons in Appendix E.

M1.justification: V3 adds an attention-pooled network variant to the studied model family and defines an l2 attention alternative. Appendix E.2 instantiates the attention variant by replacing the aggregation function. The original SUM, MEAN and MAX network procedures and training objectives remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix E.5 adds IMDB movie-rating regression and IMDB-BINARY graph classification using multisets of node degrees. These substantially broaden task and domain coverage beyond the retained point-cloud and sentiment-classification experiments. Amazon domain adaptation already appeared in v1 Appendix D.4.

E2.justification: V3 adds an attention-network comparator on ModelNet40, explicitly comparing its distance correlations in Figure 6 with the SUM/MEAN/MAX results in Figure 2. The other comparator sets remain unchanged. The stray TMD/WWL references in v1's Amazon figure caption do not establish evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix E.5 introduces direct test-set predictive evaluation using classification accuracy and regression RMSE, including node-degree preprocessing for graphs. The stated protocols for retained experiments, including training budgets, Polarity splits and 100-sample distance comparisons, remain unchanged. Complete training settings for the new benchmarks are not supplied.

E4.justification: Appendix E.2 adds a controlled aggregation-substitution analysis examining whether an attention-pooled network preserves relationships between input and representation distances. The existing insertion, noise, cardinality-shift and Amazon domain-shift analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V3 explicitly reports five repetitions with different random seeds and means with standard deviations for the new Table 3 experiments. V1 already reported uncertainty values and ten-run averaging for the cardinality-shift experiment; those practices are retained, rather than replaced by five runs.

E6.justification: Table 3 adds predictive results: NNMAX has the highest mean accuracy on ModelNet40 and Polarity, NNMEAN the lowest IMDB RMSE (0.2159), and NNSUM the highest IMDB-BINARY accuracy (70.20). Attention correlations are newly reported. Existing plotted values also change: Figure 2's EMD/NNMEAN correlation moves from 0.94 to 0.95, and Figure 3's NNMEAN bin-10 correlation from 0.94 to 0.96, although the accompanying prose retains 0.94. Table 2 and the Amazon heatmap values are unchanged.

T1.justification: V3 adds Proposition 3.3 and attention counterexamples in Appendices B.5–B.6, plus fixed-cardinality Hausdorff counterexamples. It distinguishes metrics from pseudometrics on multisets, corrects Definition 2.1 from L <= 0 to L >= 0, and revises substantive proof steps, including EMD/matching scaling and the element-addition transport construction. The original principal aggregation constants are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction expand the main contribution beyond SUM, MEAN and MAX to attention aggregation, asserting non-Lipschitz behavior under all three distances. The original claims concerning aggregation constants, network bounds, perturbations and distribution shifts remain central.

C2.justification: V3 adds metric-based aggregation-selection guidance, dataset-specific explanations for Table 3 rankings, and a bias-based explanation of NNSUM instability. It corrects the reversed robustness statement in Section 4.3 to agree with unchanged Table 2. The concluding limitations paragraph is replaced by practical discussion, although bound-looseness caveats remain elsewhere. Appendix E.2 additionally interprets attention correlations as confirming non-Lipschitz behavior.

D1.justification: V3 specifies the attention comparison network's layer arrangement and documents the node-degree multiset representation for IMDB-BINARY. The original experimental setup is retained as Appendix D with essentially unchanged hyperparameters. No new code-access, hardware or runtime information is provided.

R1.justification: A new related-work appendix substantially expands positioning around set architectures, injectivity, approximation and Lipschitz/Hölder stability. It discusses additional work including Amir et al., Davidson and Dym, and Balan et al. Section 2.4 now acknowledges prior matching-distance variants, while Section 3.1 distinguishes the analyzed attention mechanism from previously studied self-attention.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the existing prose remain intact. V3 expands explanatory passages, rewrites the conclusion as a discussion, inserts the related-work appendix, corrects terminology and cross-references, and adopts author-year citations. Existing appendices are mostly retained under new lettering.

P2.justification: V3 adds the attention Figure 6 and predictive-performance Table 3, reformats retained plots, and changes Figure 3's colors and line styles. Captions now correctly describe pairs of samples. The retained Amazon heatmaps become Figure 7 with a corrected caption, and the document adopts the ICLR template.

improvement.justification: V3 improves reliability through corrections to distance properties, transport calculations and the reversed robustness interpretation, while broader literature coverage and predictive results improve context. These gains are qualified by new weaknesses: Appendix B.6 contains inconsistent query-vector and attention-weight calculations, Appendix E.2 overstates what correlations establish about Lipschitz continuity, and Figure 3 disagrees with its retained numerical discussion. The evidence supports a limited net improvement rather than an unqualified substantial one.
